extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate or graduate students and general readers studying the history and foundations of real and complex numbers
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition and conceptual criteria for defining the arithmetic continuum (real numbers) and the extension to complex numbers, comparing Cantor (limits/sequences) and Dedekind (cuts/partitions) approaches and their consequences for analysis and algebra.

rubrics_metrics.name: Real aggregate is perfect (contains all limiting points)
rubrics_metrics.description: The aggregate of real numbers ... is perfect. It is perfect because it is closed: to all infinite processes. An infinite sequence of real numbers, if convergent, represents a real number; ... the aggregate of real numbers contains all its own limiting points and for this reason is perfect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation/example: any convergent infinite sequence of rationals that approaches a limit yields a real number (Cantor view); being closed under limits means the set contains its limit points. Anti-pattern: a domain that omits its limiting points (like rationals) is imperfect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perfect vs compact distinction and Cantor's continuum
rubrics_metrics.description: Not every compact aggregate is perfect, as the analysis of the rational domain shows; but every perfect aggregate is compact, as Cantor proves. An aggregate which is both well ordered and perfect Cantor defines as a continuum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: to be a continuum (in Cantor's sense) an aggregate must be both well ordered and perfect. Example: the real-number domain constitutes a continuum; the rational numbers, being imperfect, do not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity characterized axiomatically (Dedekind principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: If all points of a straight line fall into two classes, so that every point of the first class lies to the left of every point of the second class, then there exists one and only one point which produces this division of all points into two classes, this severing of the straight line into two portions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is presented as an axiom defining the continuity of the line (Dedekind). The passage notes it is taken as obvious and functions as a foundational postulate for constructing a continuous domain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Real numbers as Dedekind partitions (cuts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any equation, any scheme of classification, any process, which is capable of effecting such a split in the domain of rational numbers is ipso facto identified with a number, it is by definition a real number, an element of the new domain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: a 'schnitt' or partition of rationals into two non-overlapping exhaustive classes is identified with a real number. Example: partitioning rationals by those whose squares are ≤2 vs >2 yields √2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rational vs irrational Dedekind partitions distinguishing feature
rubrics_metrics.description: In the rational case, the lower class has a greatest element and the upper no least; in the irrational case, the lower class does not have a greatest element, nor yet does the upper class have a least. According to the Dedekind theory this is the only feature which distinguishes the two types of number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance/example: For rational partition at 2, the lower class includes the partition element (greatest element); for the √2 partition the cut belongs to neither class. Use this criterion to tell whether a cut yields a rational or irrational real.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence of Cantor and Dedekind constructions
rubrics_metrics.description: To any partition in the rational domain corresponds a limiting point of an infinite sequence; and conversely a limiting point of any infinite sequence can be used as an agent for the partitioning of the rational domain. All conceivable partitions on the one hand, all the limiting values of rational sequences on the other, are identical, and are just two descriptions of the same aggregate, the arithmetic continuum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: though arrived at differently (static cuts vs dynamic limits), both constructions yield the same real-number domain; proofs and mappings exist between the two descriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Closure of the real domain under infinite processes
rubrics_metrics.description: The fundamental theorem in the Cantor theory—that the domain of real numbers is closed with respect to infinite processes—also has its counterpart in the Dedekind theory: having defined the domain of reals, it is natural to inquire again whether a subsequent application of the principle would not still further extend the domain. ... The aggregate of all partitions in the rational domain is closed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: reapplication of the defining principles does not produce new magnitudes beyond the reals; both viewpoints show closure under the relevant infinite operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infinite implied even in Dedekind's static formulation
rubrics_metrics.description: A further analysis of the Dedekind procedure discloses that the infinite here is implied, even if not explicitly used. The principle of partitioning if effected upon a finite set of rational numbers would lead to trivialities ... any practical application of the principle towards the determination of an irrational number necessitates the employment of a machinery analogous to the infinite sequence of Cantor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: although Dedekind's definition avoids explicit mention of 'infinite' or 'limit', in practice infinite methods are required to calculate or approximate cuts—so the infinite intuition still underlies construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity/time intuition connection
rubrics_metrics.description: Our intuition permits us, by an act of the mind, to sever all time into the two classes, the past and the future, which are mutually exclusive and yet together comprise all of time, eternity. The now is the partition which separates all the past from all the future; ... This is what we mean by the continuity of time, by the flow of time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: Dedekind's axiom is presented as a formalization of the intuition of time's continuity. This is philosophical guidance about why the axiom is plausible, not a mathematical proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dedekind–Cantor axiom (arithmetical line / arithmetization of geometry)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is possible to assign to any point on a line a unique real number, and, conversely, any real number can be represented in a unique manner by a point on the line. This is the famous Dedekind—Cantor axiom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: adopting this axiom identifies the geometric line with the arithmetic continuum (the arithmetical line), effectively arithmetizing geometry and providing the postulate needed for analytic geometry's development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of permanence for legitimizing new number domains
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove that the Dedekind partitions are bona fide numbers it must be shown that they satisfy all the stipulations of the principle of permanence. ... The criteria of rank; the definition of operations; the proof of the associative, the commutative, and the distributive properties of these operations—all are the exact counterparts of the corresponding propositions in the Cantor theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: when extending number systems (rationals → reals → complexes), one must preserve the algebraic laws and ordering criteria (where appropriate). Use these verifications to justify that the extension behaves like a number domain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extension to complex numbers via same permanence criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: We call these Bombelli beings complex numbers, and to justify the name number we prove that they satisfy all the stipulations of the principle of permanence. ... The first stipulation is satisfied because the complex a+ib comprises the reals as a sub-domain (b = 0). The criterion of rank consists in stipulating that a+ib and c+id are equal if a=c and b=d, unequal otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: define equality componentwise, define addition and multiplication by component rules (with i^2 = -1), and verify commutativity, associativity, distributivity. This gives the complex domain legitimacy as numbers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Closure of complex numbers under rational operations
rubrics_metrics.description: As a corollary it follows that any set of rational operations performed on complex numbers leads to complex numbers. In other words, the domain of the complex is closed with respect to rational operations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: operations (addition, multiplication, etc.) on complex numbers yield complex numbers; this closure is required for the domain to be algebraically robust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex numbers amenable to analytic infinite-process notions
rubrics_metrics.description: Is it closed to the infinite processes of analysis as well? Or in other words, can we extend the notion of infinite sequence, of convergence and limit, to embrace the complex numbers too? An affirmative answer to this query was given in the nineteenth century by Gauss, Abel, Cauchy, and Weierstrass, and this fundamental fact forms the foundation of the modern theory of functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: complex numbers support limits and convergence notions; this underpins complex analysis and function theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imaginary roots occur in conjugate pairs for real-coefficient polynomials
rubrics_metrics.description: It was also known that imaginary roots of an algebraic equation with real coefficients must come in pairs, i.e., that if a+ib was a solution of such an equation, the conjugate a−ib was also one. From this it followed that an equation of odd degree must possess at least one real root.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: use conjugation symmetry to deduce existence of at least one real root for odd-degree real polynomials; example consequence for counting real vs complex roots.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor theorem connection: existence of roots ↔ polynomial factors
rubrics_metrics.description: It was surmised ... that if α be a root of an algebraic equation, then x−α is a factor in the corresponding polynomial. This fundamental fact reduced the solution of any equation to a problem in factoring, and showed conclusively that if it could be proved that any equation has a root, real or complex, it would be ipso facto established that the equation has as many roots as its degree indicates; with the reservation... multiplicity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: demonstrating root existence leads to factorization and the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra (roots counted with multiplicity). This explains why proving existence of at least one root is central.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity methods intrude into algebraic existence proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Different though these proofs are in principle, they all possess one feature in common. Somewhere, somehow,—sometimes openly, sometimes implicitly—the idea of continuity is introduced, an idea which is foreign to algebra, an idea which belongs to the realm of analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: remark that many proofs of the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra rely on continuity/analytic ideas; caution that pure algebraic arguments historically invoked analytic continuity.
